children: Norm Fosback's 'Seasonality Timing System' has one of the very best long-term track records, and suggests the market has an upside bias for the next two weeks
The stock market may be ripe for a bounce higher, at least in the short term.
You should give the stock market the benefit of the doubt for the next two weeks, according to the stock-market timing model that has the best long-term risk-adjusted track record that I know of.

This upside bias between now and the first week of December has nothing to do with the so-called Santa Claus Rally, though as I mentioned in a column two weeks ago, many will erroneously give Santa Claus credit for any rise in the market between now and early December. Instead, the next two weeks' upside bias traces to the confluence of two powerful seasonal patterns: The pre-Thanksgiving and turn-of-month seasonal tendencies.

That's according to the "Seasonality Timing System" created by Norman Fosback in the 1970s. Fosback at the time was the head of the Institute for Econometric Research. The STS is based on nothing but the calendar: Be in cash at all times except for the few days around the turns of the month and immediately prior to exchange holidays.

The pre-Thanksgiving pattern formally begins at the close of this coming Monday and ends on the Friday after Thanksgiving. Since at that point the turn-of-the-month pattern will also be in force, followers of Fosback's system will not go to cash at that point but will instead remain in the market until Dec. 4's close.

You might wonder if this period of upside bias may not materialize this year, given that it comes after the stock market's SPX DJIA COMP worst week since "liberation day" in April 2025. But history doesn't support this worry, since the pattern has appeared even in prior years that came in the middle of a severe bear market. Take the comparable two-week period in 2008, during the depths of the global financial crisis: The stock market produced a 3.5% total return during that otherwise bleak period.

There are several theories for why the STS is successful. One is that short sellers often cover their shorts before exchange holidays, since they don't want to be exposed to upside risk when trading volume is light and/or the exchanges are closed. Another is that the equity portion of investors' retirement contributions often occur around the turns of each month.

The proof of the pudding is in the eating, of course. Since the beginning of 1982, which is when my performance-auditing firm began tracking the STS, it has produced a 10.5% annualized return (through the end of October), in contrast to 12.0% annualized for buying and holding. This actually is very impressive performance, since it was produced while being in the market just a third of the time. That's why the STS, on a risk-adjusted basis, is far ahead of buying and holding.

Think about it this way: Assuming the future is like the past, with the STS you can come close to matching the market's return while sleeping like a baby two-thirds of the time. For example, the past two weeks' stock-market carnage was turned in while the STS called for being entirely in cash.

The accompanying chart is a good way of appreciating this point. It plots the STS's trailing five-year annualized return along that of buying and holding. Notice that the two are largely neck and neck - with the STS sometimes slightly ahead of the market and others slightly behind.

Though this discussion might tempt you to make a short-term bet on the market over the next two weeks, you should know that the STS is designed to be a long-term strategy. Its odds of success over any short-term period are not appreciably better than those of a coin flip.

Furthermore, you should know that, since the STS involves several dozen transactions per year, it generates lots of short-term capital gains. You therefore should consider it only in a tax-deferred account.
